| [LIT-067](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-067.md) v2 | A Social Equilibrium Existence Theorem | Debreu (1952), DOI-10.1073/pnas.38.10.886. Debreu proves existence of an equilibrium for an "abstract economy" (generalized game), in which each agent's feasible set A_ι(ā_ι) depends on the others' actions. The conditions: each action set 𝔄_ι is a contractible polyhedron; A_ι has a closed graph with non-empty compact values; f_ι is continuous on the graph into the extended reals; the value function φ_ι(ā_ι) = max f_ι is continuous; and each best-response set M_ā_ι is contractible. The proof applies the Eilenberg–Montgomery/Begle fixed-point theorem to the product best-response map. A Remark replaces the joint continuity of φ_ι with continuity (lower hemicontinuity) of A_ι plus a compact graph. A Corollary gives a saddle-point theorem that contains Kakutani's and von Neumann's. | Active — read in full 2026-09-25 ([NOTE-037](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-037.md)); the original existence theorem for generalized (constrained) games, underlying Arrow–Debreu (1954). Short, fully self-contained, and still the canonical citation. Later results (Shafer–Sonnenschein 1975; the generalized-Nash literature) weaken its hypotheses but do not supersede it as the source. |

| [LIT-481](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-481.md) | Institutions, rules, and equilibria: a unified theory | Hindriks & Guala (2015, online 2014), DOI-10.1017/S1744137414000496. Institutions are rules in equilibrium: correlated equilibria of coordination games with several equilibria, which the players represent to themselves as rules. Searle's constitutive rules ("X counts as Y in C") are obtained from a regulative rule by splitting it with a new term, a base rule (X is Y) and a status rule (if Y then Z). The new term is conservative and eliminable, so the constitutive-rules account reduces to the rules-in-equilibrium account, and Lewis's theory of theoretical terms says the term refers if the rules are true. Shown on one toy institution (first-occupancy property); general reduction asserted. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-395](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-395.md)), with the authors' reply to their six commentators in the same issue; worth reading as the shortest statement of the rules-in-equilibrium theory of institutions and of the claim that Searle's constitutive rules are regulative rules with a name added. The equilibrium half is a clear synthesis of Lewis, Aumann, Aoki and Greif. The reduction of constitutive rules is shown on one toy institution and asserted in general, and it leans on a reading of "collective acceptance" loose enough to make it hard to fail. |

| [LIT-498](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-498.md) | The Evolution of Cooperation | Axelrod & Hamilton (1981), DOI-10.1126/science.7466396. In an iterated Prisoner's Dilemma with probability w of meeting again, TIT FOR TAT won two computer tournaments (14 and 62 entries) and an ecological simulation, and no strategy can do better against it when w ≥ max((T−R)/(T−P), (T−R)/(R−S)). ALL D is always stable; reciprocity can still enter through kinship or a cluster, after which a nice stable strategy resists clusters. Applications range from cleaner fish to disease and nondisjunction. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-411](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-411.md)); worth reading as the formal statement of how reciprocity can start, spread and hold: tit-for-tat is robust in Axelrod's tournaments, cannot be bettered by any mutant when the continuation probability w is high enough, and can enter an all-defect population through kinship or clustering. "Evolutionarily stable" is stronger than what is proved: the proof shows no strategy does better than TIT FOR TAT, and always-cooperate does as well, which Boyd & Lorberbaum (1987) later turned into a proof that no pure strategy is evolutionarily stable in the repeated game. It grounds the exchange domain of morality-as-cooperation; it is not about morality. |
| [LIT-501](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-501.md) | Five Rules for the Evolution of Cooperation | Nowak (2006), DOI-10.1126/science.1133755. Five mechanisms let natural selection favour cooperators who pay c to give b: kin selection (r > c/b), direct reciprocity (w > c/b), indirect reciprocity (q > c/b), network reciprocity (b/c > k) and group selection (b/c > 1 + n/m). Each is cast as a 2×2 game, from which conditions for cooperators to be evolutionarily stable, risk-dominant or advantageous follow. Punishment is said not to be a mechanism. Cooperation is proposed as a third principle of evolution. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-409](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-409.md)), main text only; the online supplement with the derivations was not read. Worth reading as the standard short map of mechanisms for the evolution of cooperation (kin selection, direct, indirect and network reciprocity, group selection), each reduced to a benefit-to-cost threshold from a 2×2 game. Every mechanism is modelled with the donation game, so it covers altruism only: mutualism, coordination and conflict resolution, four of morality-as-cooperation's seven domains, are outside it. Its one sentence on morality credits indirect reciprocity with "the evolution of morality", citing Alexander (1987). |

| [LIT-505](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-505.md) | The Logic of Animal Conflict | Maynard Smith & Price (1973), DOI-10.1038/246015a0. Why do animals with dangerous weapons fight conventionally? | [LIT-586](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-586.md) | Précis of Breakdown of Will | Ainslie (2005), Behavioral and Brain Sciences 28(5), the précis of Breakdown of Will (2001). People and other animals discount delayed rewards hyperbolically, so preferences reverse as a smaller, sooner reward comes near, and a person becomes a population of reward-seeking "interests" that must forestall one another. Willpower is the bundling of future choices by treating the present one as a precedent: an intertemporal repeated prisoner's dilemma, not an organ or a top-down ego. The same recursion predicts the will's costs: legalism, circumscribed "lapse districts", motivated blindness to lapses, and rules that favour countable goals over subtle ones. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-443](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-443.md)), as the substitute for the 2001 book ([LIT-583](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-583.md)), which the owner suggested and which the précis follows chapter by chapter. Worth reading as the shortest complete statement of picoeconomics in Ainslie's own words. Hyperbolic discounting makes preference reverse as a smaller, sooner reward draws near, so a person behaves like a population of "interests" that bargain across time. Will is not a faculty above them but a recursive self-prediction: treating each choice as a precedent "bundles" future rewards, an intertemporal repeated prisoner's dilemma in which "credibility is power". The same mechanism predicts the will's side effects: legalism, "lapse districts", motivated misperception and compulsive over-control. |

Adds an enabling relation to a measurement scenario and reads contextuality as a game: the Experimenter chooses measurements, Nature chooses outcomes, and Nature's deterministic strategies replace the event sheaf. A causal measurement scenario adds an enabling relation (Kahn and Plotkin's information matrices renamed); Nature's deterministic strategies over it replace the event sheaf, and the Abramsky–Brandenburger definitions of empirical model and contextuality then go through unchanged. Flat scenarios and Gogioso and Pinzani's Bell scenarios with a causal order come out as special cases, and Experimenter strategies express adaptive measurement, as in the Anders–Browne GHZ OR-gate. Its sharpest point is that the strategy presheaf is not a sheaf: deterministic, compatible local strategies can fail to glue (Example 7.2) or glue non-uniquely (Example 7.3). | [LIT-966](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-966.md) v2 | Cooperative Dilemmas in Rational Debate | Handfield et al. (2025). Two debaters in a Betz-style logical space choose fixed argument strategies, with payoff w·v − d (true beliefs against changes of mind). At low and moderate truth weights the game is a cooperative dilemma: a prisoner's dilemma, stag hunt or, most often, a snowdrift in which one debater argues boldly and the other free-rides. At low weight both exit. At high weight in short debates mutual boldness is the unique, truth-optimal equilibrium. In a narrow band of mixed equilibria, raising the truth weight slightly lowers collective accuracy. All exact results are for n = 3 propositions. | Active — read 2026-10-14 ([NOTE-795](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-795.md)) in full; worth reading as a clean game-theoretic statement of epistemic free-riding in debate. Two deductive reasoners who value true beliefs but pay for each change of mind face a cooperative dilemma at low and moderate truth weights: typically one argues boldly and the other free-rides, and at low weights both exit. Read it knowing that it models two people and three propositions, that its outcome is collective accuracy and not a shared belief, and that the drop in accuracy as truth motivation rises is small and confined to a narrow band of mixed equilibria. Filed for [QUESTION-047](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-047.md); [THEORY-290](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-290.md) holds what it shows. |
| [LIT-1021](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1021.md) v2 | Bayesian Persuasion | Kamenica & Gentzkow (2011), Am. Econ. Rev. 101(6): 2590–2615. With a common prior and a signal the receiver observes and the sender commits to, any distribution of posteriors that averages to the prior can be induced. A Bayesian judge who knows the investigation was designed to convict convicts 60 percent of defendants when 70 percent are innocent. At the optimum the receiver is certain when she takes the sender's worst action and indifferent otherwise. Blackwell is not cited and manipulation is not analysed. | Active — read in full 2026-10-13 (NOTE-717) from the published AER PDF posted on Gentzkow's Stanford faculty page (web.stanford.edu/~gentzkow/research/BayesianPersuasion.pdf); the online Appendix was not read. The split pulls back the Helmholtz decomposition of the flow of unilateral payoff differences on the game graph. Potential games are exactly the games with no harmonic component. Harmonic games generically have no pure equilibrium. The nearest potential game, in a weighted l2 norm, is given in closed form. | [LIT-1484](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1484.md) | The Hive Mind is a Single Reinforcement Learning Agent | Soma, Bouteiller, Hamann and Beltrame show that in an infinite, well-mixed population, imitation of success has the expected update of a single Cross Learning bandit agent, and the weighted voter model of the honey-bee waggle dance the expected update of "Maynard-Cross Learning", π_a ← π_a + (r_k / v^π)(1[a = k] − π_a), which is the Maynard-Smith replicator dynamic. The theorem: where players can signal n bits before the result is settled, every pattern of wins and losses among 2ⁿ strategies, a cycle through all of them included, is realized. The lemma: Nash clusters are weakly ordered by population performance, and beating a population that contains a whole cluster lifts a strategy above it. The hypothesis, that real games are shaped like a spinning top, with cycles thickest at middling strength, rests on sampled empirical games. The abstract says it is proved and the body says it is not. The random-game theorem's proof is defective, and the fixed-memory fictitious play result needs a replacement rule it does not state. |

Asymptotically it does not: the discrete process is absorbed in a pure strategy profile with probability one for every learning speed. With negative payoffs the limit adds a probability-matching term to a replicator term in "benefits". | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1149](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1149.md)) from the authors' working paper of October 1995, as held in Levine's Working Paper Archive; worth reading as the proved source of "Cross learning is the replicator dynamic": a single Bush–Mosteller learner with positive payoffs moves in expectation exactly as a population under the discrete replicator dynamic, and in the continuous-time limit follows the continuous replicator dynamic on any finite horizon. Two limits matter as much as the result. Asymptotically the discrete learner is absorbed in a pure strategy profile with probability one at every learning speed, even in matching pennies where the replicator dynamic cycles; and with negative payoffs a second force, probability matching, enters beside the replicator term. |

A sketched approximation sets the clamp to the expected action rather than zero; in a 60-agent bar problem, clamping to the average action learned best across attendance levels, clamping to absence close behind, and G itself worst. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1153](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1153.md)) from the NASA Technical Reports Server copy (document 20010066523, a 7-page scanned report marked public use permitted), not the version in the Intelligent Agent Technology proceedings; worth reading as the most compact statement the record holds of difference rewards. | [LIT-1508](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1508.md) | Re-evaluating Evaluation | Balduzzi, Tuyls, Pérolat & Graepel (NeurIPS 2018). Evaluation data are antisymmetric matrices: Elo is their row mean in logit space, exact only when the log-odds are curl-free, and inflatable by copies; the Schur decomposition gives a multidimensional Elo for cyclic interactions. Nash averaging scores agents (and tasks) against the maximum-entropy Nash equilibrium of a zero-sum meta-game, which ignores exact copies when that equilibrium is unique. Applied to Atari, human ties with the best agents. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1155](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1155.md)) from arXiv v2 (30 October 2018, the authors' "NIPS 2018, final version"); worth reading as the source of the Hodge and Schur reading of evaluation data and of Nash averaging. Elo is the row mean of the log-odds matrix, exact only when the log-odds have no cyclic part, and copies of an agent move it. Nash averaging scores each agent against the maximum-entropy Nash team of the meta-game. Its invariance to copies is proved only for the Nash set (Lemma 1): when the meta-game has more than one equilibrium, copying an agent moves the maximum-entropy selection and the Nash averages with it, which the reading checked by script. | [LIT-1509](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1509.md) | Open-ended Learning in Symmetric Zero-sum Games | Balduzzi, Garnelo, Bachrach, Czarnecki, Pérolat, Jaderberg & Graepel (ICML 2019). Every symmetric zero-sum game between parametrized agents splits into a transitive part and a cyclic part relative to a measure on agents. In cyclic games individual performance is meaningless, so the paper measures populations, by the value of the game between them and by the convex hull of their evaluation rows (the gamescape). Response to the Nash mixture enlarges the gamescape, and response to the rectified Nash, which trains each supported agent on what it beats, grows it in Blotto-type games where self-play does not. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1143](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1143.md)) from arXiv v2 (13 May 2019, the authors' "ICML 2019, final version"); worth reading for one invariant and one reframing. The invariant: the value of the zero-sum game between two populations, which does not depend on the choice of Nash, ignores members that are behavioural mixtures of others, and cannot be positive for a population inside another's hull. The reframing: in a cyclic game an individual agent's performance means nothing, so progress is the growth of a population's gamescape. On 310 random 3×3 matrix games it learned the optimum in all, VDN and QMIX failed in 177; it also did better on Gaussian squeeze and a penalised predator-prey task. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1141](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1141.md)) from arXiv v1 (14 May 2019, the ICML version with its supplement, arXiv non-exclusive licence); worth reading for the Individual-Global-Max condition, that the agents' individually greedy actions form a greedy joint action, and for showing it strictly weaker than additive or monotonic factorisation. | [LIT-1511](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1511.md) | Frequency adjusted multi-agent Q-learning | Kaisers & Tuyls (AAMAS 2010). The replicator-plus-entropy model of Boltzmann Q-learning derived by Tuyls et al. In Q-learning only the chosen action's value is updated, so E[Q̇_i] carries a factor x_i, and trajectories in the prisoners' dilemma, battle of the sexes and matching pennies deviate from the model, depending on initialization. Frequency Adjusted Q-learning scales each update by min(β/x_i, 1) and follows the model wherever x_i ≥ β. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1140](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1140.md)) from the AAMAS 2010 proceedings PDF on the IFAAMAS site; read in place of Tuyls, Verbeeck & Lenaerts 2003 ([LIT-1501](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1501.md)), whose model it restates and corrects. Worth reading as the correction to "Q-learning is replicator dynamics plus mutation": the selection–mutation equation describes Q-learning with Boltzmann exploration only if every action's estimate is updated at the same rate. In Q-learning the chosen action is updated more often, so the expected change of Q_i carries a factor x_i, and the learning traces depart from the model, depending on how the Q-values are initialized. Frequency Adjusted Q-learning divides the step by x_i and matches the model. Evidence is three 2×2 games, plotted, with no quantitative measure of fit. |
| [LIT-1512](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1512.md) | Mean Field Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning | Yang, Luo, Li, Zhou, Zhang & Wang (2018). Factorizing each agent's Q-function into pairwise terms and expanding about the neighbours' mean action reduces many-agent interaction to an agent against the average of its neighbours. Mean field Q-learning and actor-critic follow; MF-Q is proved to converge to the Nash Q-value under strong assumptions. With 500 and 1000 agents in Gaussian Squeeze the mean field methods learn where four baselines fail; MF-Q reproduces the order parameter of a 20 × 20 Ising model against MCMC; and it wins a 64-versus-64 battle game. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1148](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1148.md)) from arXiv v5 (15 December 2020), the ICML 2018 paper with appendices; worth reading as the standard way multi-agent RL reaches hundreds of agents: each agent's Q-function takes its own action and the mean action of its neighbours, so many-body interaction becomes a two-body one between an agent and the average of the rest. Mean field Q-learning is proved to converge to a Nash Q-value under strong assumptions, every stage game met in training having a global optimum or a saddle point among them, and learns where four baselines fail with 500 and 1000 agents. The approximation needs agents that are homogeneous and interchangeable within a neighbourhood; the bound on its error is loose and the cancellation of errors argued, not proved; and the contraction step needs a high Boltzmann temperature while the convergence assumptions need it to go to zero. |
| [LIT-1513](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1513.md) | Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning in Sequential Social Dilemmas | Leibo, Zambaldi, Lanctot, Marecki & Graepel (2017). Defines a sequential social dilemma as a Markov game whose cooperative and defecting policies, played against each other, give payoffs satisfying the social dilemma inequalities. Both games embed Prisoner's Dilemmas, but network size raises defection in Gathering and lowers it in Wolfpack, which no matrix game captures. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1151](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1151.md)) from arXiv v1, the AAMAS 2017 paper; worth reading as the paper that moved social dilemmas from matrix games to learned policies in Markov games. | [LIT-1516](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1516.md) | α-Rank: Multi-Agent Evaluation by Evolution | Omidshafiei, Papadimitriou, Piliouras, Tuyls, Rowland, Lespiau, Czarnecki, Lanctot, Pérolat & Munos (Scientific Reports 2019). It ranks strategy profiles by the stationary distribution of a finite-population, rare-mutation imitation chain, unique at every finite ranking intensity α. As α grows its transitions become those of Markov chains on the sink strongly connected components of the better-response graph. The paper calls these sinks Markov-Conley chains and ties them to the chain components of the replicator flow. The large-α limit of the stationary distribution, and so the selection among several sinks, is not characterized. | [LIT-1517](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1517.md) | Counterfactual Multi-Agent Policy Gradients | Foerster, Farquhar, Afouras, Nardelli & Whiteson train decentralised actors with one centralised critic Q(s, τ, u) and credit agent a with A^a = Q(s, τ, u) − Σ_{u′a} π^a(u′a \| τ^a) Q(s, τ, (u^−a, u′a)): the value of the joint action against the critic's average over a's own alternatives under a's policy, the others' actions fixed. The counterfactual values are the learned critic's estimates, which exist only for actions the agents sometimes take, so the method credits agents that all act on every step and does not recover the value of one that is never heeded. | [LIT-1518](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1518.md) | Eliciting Informative Feedback: The Peer-Prediction Method | Miller, Resnick & Zeckhauser (2005). A center with no independent information scores each rater by applying a strictly proper scoring rule to the distribution of a reference rater's report that her own report implies, given a common prior and signal model. Truthful reporting is a strict Nash equilibrium; scaling the scores induces costly effort and can outweigh bribes; three or more raters allow budget balance. Uninformative equilibria also exist, and collusion, risk aversion, unmodelled private signals and trust in the center are named limits. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1139](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1139.md)) from the authors' final pre-publication draft of 26 January 2005, on Paul Resnick's University of Michigan page; worth reading as the founding scoring rule for evaluators when there is no ground truth. Each rater reports a signal, the center turns it into a posterior over a reference rater's report, and the rater is paid a strictly proper scoring rule on that posterior against what the reference rater actually reported. Truth-telling is then a strict Nash equilibrium (Proposition 1), and scaling the payments buys effort. It is not the only equilibrium: everyone always reporting h, or always l, is an equilibrium too, and collusion is named as a limit the paper does not settle. The mechanism needs a common prior and a signal model the center knows. |
| [LIT-1519](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1519.md) | Learning with Opponent-Learning Awareness | Foerster et al. replace an agent's objective V¹(θ¹, θ²) with its value after the opponent's anticipated naive gradient step, V¹(θ¹, θ² + Δθ²), and differentiate through Δθ² = η∇θ²V², adding (∇θ²V¹)ᵀ∇θ¹∇θ²V² · δη to the naive gradient. A policy-gradient version cooperated in the Coin Game, and with opponent modelling did so less reliably. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1150](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1150.md)) from arXiv v4 (19 September 2018, the AAMAS 2018 text, arXiv non-exclusive licence); worth reading as the first learning rule that models another learner's update and climbs its own return through it: a LOLA agent adds to its gradient the effect of its own parameters on the opponent's next naive step. In the limit where learning is slow relative to play, each agent's choice distribution follows ẋ_i/x_i = β[(Ay)_i − x·Ay] + α Σ_j x_j log(x_j/x_i): a coupled replicator dynamic plus an entropy-like term towards uniform play. With α = 0 it is the conservative two-population replicator equation; with α > 0 it is dissipative. In rock–scissors–paper, simulations show quasiperiodic tori and Hamiltonian chaos without decay, and limit cycles, intermittency and chaotic attractors with it. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1144](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1144.md)) from arXiv:nlin/0204057v2 (18 August 2002); worth reading as a four-page derivation of the learning dynamics of softmax reinforcement learners with forgetting: two such agents follow coupled replicator equations plus a term α_X Σ_j x_j log(x_j/x_i), set by the rate at which reward memories decay, that pushes each agent towards uniform play. Without forgetting the system is conservative, Hamiltonian in zero-sum games, and in rock–scissors–paper it is chaotic for nonzero tie rewards; with forgetting it is dissipative, with limit cycles and chaotic attractors. The memory update is not Watkins's Q-learning: every action's memory is updated with its average reward at the same rate. |
| [LIT-1521](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1521.md) | A Simple Adaptive Procedure Leading to Correlated Equilibrium | Hart & Mas-Colell (Econometrica 2000; handout 1996). Regret matching: each period a player who last played j switches to k with probability R_t(j, k)/μ, the positive part of its average gain had it played k whenever it played j, and otherwise repeats j. If all players do so, the empirical distribution of play converges almost surely to the set of correlated equilibria. The proof runs through Blackwell's approachability theorem; regrets vanish exactly when the empirical distribution approaches the correlated-equilibrium set. Inertia, a positive probability of repeating, is needed for the result. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1142](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1142.md)) from the published article as posted on Sergiu Hart's homepage; worth reading as the theorem that correlated equilibrium is reachable by simple adaptive play: if every player switches from its last action to each alternative with probability proportional to its positive regret for not having made that switch in the past, the empirical joint distribution of play converges almost surely to the set of correlated equilibria. No device, no forecasts and no best replies are needed; the common history is the correlating device. The limits matter: convergence is to the set, not to a point; correlated equilibria that are interior and not pure Nash cannot be the limit of the empirical distribution; and the players must observe one another's past play. |
| [LIT-1524](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1524.md) v2 | Cleaning up the neighborhood: A full classification for adversarial partial monitoring | Lattimore & Szepesvári (2018; ALT 2019). Completes the classification of finite adversarial partial-monitoring games by minimax regret to all games, including the degenerate ones (with actions optimal only on a lower-dimensional part of the simplex) that Bartók et al. (2014) left open: 0 with no pair of neighbouring actions, Θ̃(√n) when locally observable, Θ(n^2/3) when globally but not locally observable, and Ω(n) otherwise. A new NeighborhoodWatch2 attains √n with high probability by redistributing mass onto degenerate actions in proportion to the neighbours they lie between. It corrects a slip in Bartók et al.'s T^2/3 lower-bound proof and, in the preprint's words, an exchanged expectation and maximum in the earlier localisation argument. A second algorithm, RelExp3, gives point-locally observable games an asymptotic √n bound free of arbitrarily large game constants, with a matching linear dependence on the number of feedback symbols. | Active — read 2026-10-25 ([NOTE-1162](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1162.md)) in full, from the arXiv preprint v1 of 23 May 2018 (arxiv.org/pdf/1805.09247v1, 24 pp.); the ALT 2019 version (PMLR 98:529–556) was fetched and its theorem statements, footnote and contribution list compared, not read in full. Worth reading for the completed classification of finite adversarial partial-monitoring games, degenerate and duplicate actions included ([THEORY-963](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-963.md)); for how actions that are optimal only on a boundary enter it, through the neighbourhood set and not as neighbours, and for its correction of the lower-bound proof of Bartók et al. (2014) ([THEORY-961](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-961.md)); for NeighborhoodWatch2, a simpler algorithm with a high-probability √n bound; and for RelExp3 on point-locally observable games ([THEORY-950](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-950.md)). Read it knowing that the arXiv text says Foster and Rakhlin and Bartók et al. "inadvertently exchanged an expectation and maximum" in their localisation argument and the published text no longer says so, though both abstracts say "correct errors in previous analyses"; that it proves only the two pieces of the classification that were missing or flawed and cites the rest; that its constants are game-dependent and can be large; and that a few small typos survive in the arXiv text. |
| [LIT-1526](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1526.md) v2 | Online Learning and Blackwell Approachability with Partial Monitoring: Optimal Convergence Rates | Kwon & Perchet (2017). Blackwell approachability generalizes regret minimization (multi-criteria optimization, online optimization of a convex loss, online linear optimization under a cumulative constraint). Under partial monitoring the decision maker does not see outcomes but a random signal correlated with the decision–outcome pair, or with the outcome only. The paper gives the first approachability algorithms for polytope target sets with convergence rate O(T^-1/2) when the signal does not depend on the decision and O(T^-1/3) for general signals, and shows that these rates cannot be improved without further assumptions on the objectives or the signals (abstract). | Active — read 2026-10-25 ([NOTE-1159](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1159.md)) in full, from the PMLR copy and its supplementary material; worth reading for the reduction of approachability under partial monitoring to full-information approachability in a lifted space of flags, for the optimal worst-case rates, O(T^-1/3) for general signals and O(T^-1/2) when the signal does not depend on the decision ([THEORY-947](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-947.md)), and for the exploration floor that decision-dependent signals require ([THEORY-957](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-957.md)). Read it knowing that approachability is assumed rather than decided, that the guarantees concern the average payoff and so let violations be compensated over time, that optimality is worst case over games, that the constants grow with a simplicial subdivision, and that the proof for outcome-dependent signals is omitted. |
| [LIT-1528](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1528.md) v3 | Partial Monitoring—Classification, Regret Bounds, and Algorithms | Bartók, Foster, Pál, Rakhlin & Szepesvári (2014). In a partial-monitoring game the learner picks an action, the environment an outcome, and the learner suffers a loss and receives a feedback signal, both fixed functions of action and outcome. For every game with finitely many actions and outcomes (against adversarial opponents, every non-degenerate one) the minimax regret is zero or scales as T^1/2, T^2/3 or T, up to constants and logarithmic factors; computationally efficient algorithms attain it within a logarithmic factor, with individual bounds on expected regret for i.i.d. outcomes (abstract). | Active — read 2026-10-25 ([NOTE-1164](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1164.md)) in full, from the authors' preprint of March 2013 on Alexander Rakhlin's MIT page; worth reading for the complete classification of finite partial-monitoring games by minimax regret (0, Θ̃(√T), Θ(T^2/3), Θ(T); [THEORY-964](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-964.md)), for the linear-algebra conditions, global and local observability, that decide the class ([THEORY-962](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-962.md)), and for the algorithms CBP and NeighborhoodWatch. Read it knowing that the adversarial classification covers non-degenerate games only, that Lattimore and Szepesvári (2019, LIT-1524) completed it to degenerate games, corrected the kernel in its T^2/3 lower-bound proof, and, in their preprint, an exchanged expectation and maximum in NeighborhoodWatch's localisation (THEORY-963, THEORY-961), that the classification concerns the best policy in a fixed, known game, and that the copy read is the preprint, not the journal text. |
| [LIT-1603](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1603.md) | The Evolution of Cooperation | Sachs, Mueller, Wilcox & Bull (2004). A tripartite framework for how cooperation within and between species evolves and is maintained: directed reciprocation, shared genes (kin selection) and byproduct benefits, each subdivided. Plant–rhizobium and squid–Vibrio symbioses are fitted to it, and natural systems often combine models. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-27, not read. Registered in the second pass on the exchange of 2026-10-27, "Repository coverage assessment", at the owner's request to find what it mentioned and did not cite (second curation entry of 2026-10-27). No NOTE is filed. |
